design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison of five groups of 30 recruited from the unit's participant database and by snowball sampling: frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week), infrequent use (less than four times a week but at least once a month), ex-ketamine (abstinent at least 1 month), polydrug controls matched to the current-use groups on other drugs, and controls who did not use illicit drugs. One drug-free session, at least 24 hours after any psychotropic drug, with CANTAB tasks, a source memory task, prose recall, fluency, the Hayling test and self-report symptom scales; hair analysis (3 cm, about 3 months) for ketamine. One-way ANOVAs with Bonferroni post hoc tests (p. 80).
can_establish: Whether, at one time point, people with frequent, infrequent or past ketamine use differed from each other and from polydrug and non-drug controls on the tasks and symptom scales used, within this convenience sample.
cannot_establish: Whether ketamine caused any difference (there are no data from before use, and the frequent group had about 3 fewer years of education, a lower premorbid IQ estimate and more family history of mental illness, none of them adjusted for in the group comparisons); whether the frequent group's differences are lasting or short-lived after-effects (it was tested a mean of 1.6 days after last use); or whether deficits reverse after stopping, because the ex-ketamine group is a different set of people, most of whom had used less.

sample.recruitment: The unit's existing database of participants and snowball sampling (p. 78). All participants were paid; the institutional ethics committee approved the study (p. 78).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Groups defined by self-reported frequency (p. 78): frequent, more than four times a week; infrequent, less than four times a week but at least once a month; ex-ketamine, abstinent for at least 1 month (12 previously frequent, 8 formerly daily); polydrug controls matched with the current-use groups for other drugs; non-drug controls taking no illicit drugs. Drug-using participants had to abstain from psychotropic drugs for at least 24 hours before testing, and all had to have no history of head injury or organic brain damage and English as native language (p. 78). How many people were screened or excluded is not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a single session; all 150 completed (p. 80).
sample.selection_effects: Convenience sample drawn from the research unit's own database and participants' networks, with group membership by self-reported frequency, checked against hair ketamine but without stated criteria for exclusion. The frequent group differs from the others in education, premorbid IQ estimate and family history of mental illness; the polydrug group had the highest premorbid IQ estimate and the non-drug group one of the lowest. The current-use groups are people still using; people who stopped because of problems could appear in the ex-ketamine group or not be recruited at all. Group sizes were fixed at 30, so the sample says nothing about how common these patterns of use are.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug history; urine samples analysed (Medscreen) but results not reported; hair samples (3 cm, about the previous 3 months; Trichotech) analysed for ketamine and said to confirm self-reported other drug use (pp. 78, 80–81). Correlations used self-reported amount per session because hair indices were considered somewhat unreliable (p. 80).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported (Table 2, p. 81). Frequent group: 3.80 (2.36) g per session on 20.13 (2.36) days per month, last use 1.6 (1.27) days before testing (range 1–7), 6.07 (4.89) years of use; 19 reported using ketamine daily (p. 80). Infrequent group: 1.28 (1.13) g on 3.25 (2.55) days per month, last use 11.3 (9.36) days before testing, 4.20 (2.20) years. Ex-ketamine group: 1.49 (2.00) g on 2.55 (3.90) days per month just before stopping, abstinent 344.43 (624.72) days (range 120–2980), 7.63 (2.63) years of use; 8 had used daily, and the group's peak frequency was 11.21 (9.34) days per month (p. 80). In the first 2 months of use all three groups reported 0.50 to 0.62 g per session; age at first use 19.83 (8.21), 21.17 (6.01) and 20.03 (5.03) years. Hair ketamine 282.14 (566.53), 18.01 (41.06) and 3.55 (13.63) ng/mm; none detected in either control group. Route and purity not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Regular use (more than 10 times a year; Table 3, p. 81) of cannabis by 21, 21, 21 and 29 of 30 in the frequent, infrequent, ex-ketamine and polydrug groups; ecstasy 20, 28, 19, 22; cocaine 21, 26, 19, 22; amphetamine 13, 16, 4, 9; alcohol 29, 29, 25, 26 and 29 (including the non-drug group). The authors report no differences between the four drug-using groups in self-reported amounts or frequencies (p. 81), but the proportions of people with regular use differ (editors' calculation: χ²(3) = 8.9, P = 0.03 for cannabis; 8.5, P = 0.04 for ecstasy; 11.9, P = 0.008 for amphetamine). Table 4 (p. 82) shows that more people in the ketamine groups than in the polydrug group had used or tried 2CB, 2C-I, DMT, GHB or nitrous oxide (for example, 2CB tried by 16 in the frequent group and none of the polydrug controls). No drug other than ketamine was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 24 hours from psychotropic drugs for drug-using participants, by self-report; urine results are not reported, and the follow-up paper on the same participants states that the 24 hours could not be verified biologically (Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 132). Cigarettes were allowed in the hourly 10-minute breaks (p. 79). The frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days (mean 1.6) after last ketamine use (Table 2, p. 81); the follow-up paper gives 2 (SD 2.60) days for the same session (reporting issue 8).

comparison.controls: 30 polydrug controls (no ketamine detected in hair) matched to the current-use groups on other drug use, and 30 controls who did not use illicit drugs (29 of them regular drinkers), recruited in the same way (pp. 78, 80–81).
comparison.matching: Matched on other drugs by design (self-reported amounts and frequencies did not differ, but the proportions of people with regular use did; see polysubstance); age and sex similar; education, premorbid IQ estimate and family history of mental illness differ and are not adjusted for.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No cognitive or psychiatric measurement before use; premorbid ability only as a current reading-based estimate, which was lowest in the frequent group. Childhood trauma was not measured; the authors note it as a risk factor for dissociation (p. 86).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The polydrug controls used cannabis (29 regular), ecstasy, cocaine, alcohol and amphetamine at rates similar to or higher than the ketamine groups but had less experience of other hallucinogens and dissociatives (Table 4); the non-drug controls used alcohol only.

outcomes.instruments: All measured in a drug-free session; nothing was measured during intoxication. CANTAB pattern recognition memory (percentage correct), spatial working memory (errors and strategy score) and Stockings of Cambridge (problems solved in the minimum number of moves); a source memory task (80 low-frequency words heard in a male or female voice, recognition after a filled 6-minute delay; recognition d′, bias C and source accuracy); Rivermead prose recall, immediately and after about 10 minutes; category (fruit or vegetables) and letter (M or B) fluency in 90 seconds; the Hayling test of response initiation and inhibition; spot-the-word as a premorbid IQ estimate. Self-reports: the short Oxford–Liverpool Inventory of Feelings and Experiences (unusual experiences, cognitive disorganization, introvertive anhedonia, impulsive non-conformity, rated for daily life when not under the influence of drugs), the Peters et al. Delusions Inventory (total, distress, preoccupation, conviction), the Dissociative Experiences Scale, the Beck Depression Inventory and the Spielberger trait anxiety scale (pp. 79–80).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard published tasks and scales, but no comparison with norms: impairment means a lower score than other groups in this sample. The scoring of the Dissociative Experiences Scale is not described (group means 321 to 784).
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment or elevation means a significant one-way ANOVA followed by a Bonferroni post hoc difference from other groups (p. 80). No clinical threshold is applied, except that the Discussion calls the frequent group's mean depression score mild to moderate (p. 85) without giving cut-offs.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni within each ANOVA's post hoc comparisons only; no correction across the 25 outcome scores (14 cognitive and 11 self-report) or across the correlations, whose number is not stated.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the drug history was taken at the start of each session (p. 78), so testers knew group membership.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means and SDs for most measures (Tables 5–6, pp. 83–84); spatial working memory errors, pattern recognition and the O-LIFE subscales appear only as bar charts (Figures 1–3). Omnibus F(4, 145): SWM errors 8.05 and strategy 5.00; Stockings 6.58; pattern recognition 6.37 (all P < 0.001); d′ 2.74 (P = 0.031); PDI total 8.40 and DES 6.60 (P < 0.001); BDI 3.04 (P = 0.019); unusual experiences 6.12, cognitive disorganization 4.81 and impulsive non-conformity 3.96 (pp. 81–84). Correlations in the frequent group: PDI total with current amount per session r = 0.433 (P = 0.019); d′ with spot-the-word r = 0.474 (P = 0.009) (p. 84). Editors' calculation, frequent group against polydrug controls (pooled SD, n = 30 each; 95% CI by the large-sample approximation): Stockings d ≈ −1.18 (−1.73 to −0.63); SWM strategy 0.66 (0.14 to 1.18); d′ −0.65 (−1.17 to −0.13); PDI total 0.81 (0.29 to 1.34); DES 0.75 (0.23 to 1.28); BDI 0.62 (0.10 to 1.14); category fluency 0.10 (−0.41 to 0.60). Fisher z 95% CI for r = 0.433 with n = 30: 0.09 to 0.69.
analysis.covariates: None in the group comparisons. Spot-the-word and years of education were examined only by correlation within the frequent group (p. 84).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract lists a simple vigilance task that appears in neither the Method nor the Results. Spatial working memory errors, pattern recognition and the O-LIFE subscales are shown only in figures. The number of correlations run is not stated, and one significant correlation with ketamine use is reported. Urine results and hair results for drugs other than ketamine are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. Thirty per group gives reasonable power for large differences between two groups, but little for the pattern across five groups on which the conclusions about infrequent and past use rely.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one session, the frequent ketamine group, tested about 1.6 days after last use and with fewer years of education and a lower premorbid IQ estimate, made more spatial working memory errors, had a poorer search strategy, solved fewer Stockings problems, recognised fewer patterns and had lower word-recognition d′ than the other groups; prose recall, letter and category fluency, the Hayling test and source memory did not differ. The infrequent and ex-ketamine groups did not differ from controls on any cognitive measure. The frequent group scored highest on delusional ideation, dissociation, unusual experiences and depression; the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups scored above the non-drug controls on some of these, but are not reported to differ from the polydrug controls.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the frequent group was impaired on category fluency, which the Results contradict (p. 82; Table 5, p. 83). It concludes that frequent use is associated with impairments and reduced wellbeing, and that the cognitive impairments may be reversible on stopping because the ex-ketamine group showed none, whereas “delusional symptoms persist” (p. 77). Reversibility is inferred from different people: the ex-ketamine group had used less before stopping (2.55 days per month, peak 11.21) than the frequent group (20.13), and the authors themselves state that only retesting the frequent group after abstinence could show it (p. 86). The persistence of delusions rests on the ex-ketamine group's PDI total exceeding the non-drug controls' (P < 0.01 as printed), a difference that cannot be reproduced from Table 6 (editors' calculation) and was not shown against the polydrug controls, whose mean was close (13.03 vs 15.79). The argument that symptoms rising with ketamine use tell against pre-existing differences (p. 85) relies on a gradient across groups that also differ in education and family history and on one correlation (r = 0.433) out of an unstated number. The Discussion's statement that groups were matched for other drug use objectively by hair analysis (p. 85) is not backed by reported hair data for other drugs. The Summary's “broad-ranging cognitive impairments” (p. 86) overstates differences found on four of the tasks, and the authors' own suggestion that these might reflect withdrawal (p. 86) cannot be excluded with testing 1 to 7 days after last use.

timeline.event: Frequent and infrequent ketamine groups tested on the night of use and 3 days later: on day 3 the frequent group was more impaired on episodic and semantic memory tasks

Three-year follow-up of 18 people who had cut down their ketamine use: category fluency no longer different from polydrug controls, but prose recall lower and digit cancellation slower at both sessions; prose recall did not differ in the present study

One-year follow-up of 119 of these 150 participants: the frequent group's spatial working memory errors and pattern recognition differed from other groups averaged over both sessions, but its follow-up means approached the controls'; its Stockings and strategy scores improved to control levels; delusional ideation and dissociation remained highest in the frequent group; depression scores rose in the frequent and abstinent groups

replication.where_it_stands: The only later data read for this card come from the same participants' 1-year follow-up (Morgan et al., 2010b), which tests the stability of these differences rather than replicating them in an independent sample; there, some differences persisted (delusional ideation, dissociation, averaged cognitive differences) and others resolved (planning and strategy). Earlier studies from the same unit reported prose recall deficits that this study did not find, which the authors attribute to the earlier testing designs (p. 85). Later independent studies were not searched by this reader, so the status is provisional.

funding.funder: Grant to H.V.C. and C.J.A.M. from the UK Economic and Social Research Council (RES-000-23-0945) (Acknowledgements, p. 86).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London; participants were recruited partly from the unit's own database (p. 78).

what_would_settle_it: Repeated testing of the same people before and after they stop using ketamine, with abstinence verified biologically, alongside people who continue, with education, premorbid ability, family history and other hallucinogen use adjusted for, testers blind to group, and an interval since last use long enough to separate lasting effects from after-effects of recent use or withdrawal.

domains.note: Education (12.27 vs about 15 years), premorbid IQ estimate and family history of mental illness differ, and none is adjusted for; other hallucinogens and dissociatives were used more in the ketamine groups; the polydrug matching holds for self-reported amounts but not for the proportions of people with regular use.

Self-reported use, checked against hair ketamine but with no stated thresholds or exclusions; ketamine was found in the ex-ketamine group's hair despite reported abstinence of at least 120 days; urine results not reported; the frequent group's frequency figures are internally inconsistent (see reporting issues).

Convenience sample from the unit's database and participants' networks; current-use groups are people still using, and people who stopped because of problems may be under- or over-represented in the ex-ketamine group.

The frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days after last use, so after-effects or withdrawal may contribute, as the authors note (p. 86); whether the ex-ketamine group stopped with treatment is not reported.
All 150 completed the session; no missing data are reported.
Standard tasks and scales, but testers were not blind to group, the symptom measures are self-reports, and the scoring of the Dissociative Experiences Scale is not described.

The abstract contradicts the Results on category fluency and names a vigilance task that is never reported; several post hoc differences on which the conclusions rest cannot be reproduced from the printed tables, and two recomputed F values differ from those printed; several measures appear only in figures; the number of correlations is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The frequent group's lower scores on the CANTAB tasks and d′ and its higher symptom scores are sizeable and measured with standard instruments, but uncorrected differences in education, premorbid ability and family history, and testing only 1 to 7 days after last use, prevent attributing them to lasting effects of ketamine; and the pattern of post hoc differences on which the claims about infrequent and past use rest is not reproducible from the printed tables. The source may be cited for the frequent group's lower performance on spatial working memory, planning, pattern recognition and word recognition, and higher delusional ideation, dissociation and depression scores, relative to this sample's other groups, with the confounders named, and for the absence of cognitive differences in the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups; it should not be cited for reversibility, for delusions persisting after stopping, for a category fluency deficit, or for causation.

key_findings.finding: Groups did not differ in age or sex, but the frequent ketamine group had fewer years of education (12.27 (4.84) vs 15.33 (2.56) in the infrequent and 15.10 (2.47) in the non-drug group; F(4, 145) = 4.07, P = 0.004; post hoc P = 0.018 and 0.04), a lower premorbid IQ estimate (spot-the-word 45.67 (6.13) vs 50.90 (4.09) infrequent, P = 0.04, and 51.53 (4.22) polydrug, P = 0.01; F(4, 145) = 7.29, P < 0.001) and more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 vs 1 to 3 of 30 in the other groups; χ²(4) = 12.59, P = 0.013).
key_findings.note: No first-degree relative with schizophrenia was reported in any group (p. 78). The polydrug group also scored higher than the non-drug group on spot-the-word (P = 0.028). Table 1 gives 22 men and 10 women in the polydrug group, 32 for a group of 30 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Self-reported ketamine use: the frequent group used 3.80 (2.36) g per session on 20.13 (2.36) days per month, last 1.6 (1.27) days before testing (range 1–7), and 19 of 30 reported daily use; the infrequent group 1.28 (1.13) g on 3.25 (2.55) days, last 11.3 (9.36) days before testing; the ex-ketamine group 1.49 (2.00) g on 2.55 (3.90) days per month just before stopping, abstinent for 344.43 (624.72) days (range 120–2980), 8 of whom had once used daily, with a group peak of 11.21 (9.34) days per month. All three groups reported 0.50 to 0.62 g per session in their first 2 months of use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 2nd paragraph (p. 80); Table 2 (p. 81)
key_findings.note: A mean of 20.13 days per month with an SD of 2.36 cannot be reconciled with daily use by 19 of 30 (see reporting issues). Amount, frequency and days since last use differed between the frequent and infrequent groups (Z = 1.81, 3.87 and 2.84), with two Z–P pairs inconsistent (see reporting issues). The follow-up paper gives 2 (SD 2.60) days since last use for the frequent group at this same session (reporting issue 8).

key_findings.finding: Hair analysis (3 cm, about the previous 3 months) showed ketamine at 282.14 (566.53) ng/mm in the frequent, 18.01 (41.06) in the infrequent and 3.55 (13.63) in the ex-ketamine group (group difference F(4, 149) = 6.70, P < 0.001), and none in the hair of any participant in either control group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 1st paragraph (p. 80); Table 2 (p. 81)
key_findings.note: The ex-ketamine group's shortest reported abstinence (120 days) exceeds the window of a 3-cm sample, yet its mean is above zero; the paper does not comment and gives no thresholds for classifying participants by hair. With 150 participants in five groups the df should be 4,145.

key_findings.finding: Groups differed in spatial working memory errors (F(4, 145) = 8.05, P < 0.001) and strategy score (F(4, 145) = 5.00, P < 0.001): the frequent ketamine group made more errors than the others (P < 0.01) and had a poorer, that is higher, strategy score than all other groups (32.73 (5.77) against 26.53 to 28.93; P < 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Spatial working memory (Fig. 1) (p. 81, continuing on p. 82); Figure 1 (p. 82); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: Error means appear only in Figure 1 (editors' reading: about 32 errors in the frequent group against about 11 to 19 in the others). Editors' calculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): the strategy difference from the polydrug controls (32.73 vs 28.93) gives P ≈ 0.11.

key_findings.finding: The frequent group solved fewer Stockings of Cambridge problems in the minimum number of moves than every other group (7.66 (1.61) against 8.89 to 9.53; F(4, 145) = 6.58; post hoc P < 0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Stockings of Cambridge (Table 5) (p. 82); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: The omnibus P is printed as < 0.00. Editors' calculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): P ≈ 0.03 against the ex-ketamine group and below 0.002 against the others; d ≈ −1.18 (95% CI −1.73 to −0.63) against the polydrug controls.

key_findings.finding: The frequent group recognised fewer patterns on the pattern recognition memory task than all other groups (F(4, 145) = 6.37, P < 0.001; post hoc P < 0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Pattern recognition memory (Fig. 2) (p. 82); Figure 2 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: Means appear only in Figure 2, whose axis starts at 75% (editors' reading: about 83% correct in the frequent group against about 90 to 95% in the others).

key_findings.finding: Word-recognition discriminability (d′) on the source memory task differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 2.74, P = 0.031): frequent 2.36 (0.74), infrequent 2.74 (0.73), ex-ketamine 2.97 (0.63), polydrug 2.85 (0.76) and non-drug 2.67 (0.82); the paper reports the frequent group as lower than all other groups (P < 0.05). Bias (C) and the proportion of source errors did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Source memory task (Table 5) (p. 82); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reaches P < 0.05 (P ≈ 0.02); against the non-drug controls P ≈ 0.11 even without correction. Within the frequent group d′ correlated with spot-the-word (r = 0.474, P = 0.009; p. 84).

key_findings.finding: There were no group differences in prose recall (only a main effect of delay, F(1, 145) = 34.37, P < 0.001; group means 8.11 to 8.32 idea units immediately and 7.20 to 7.83 after the delay), letter fluency (15.14 to 17.53 words), category fluency (14.73 to 17.27; frequent group 16.84 (4.80), non-drug controls 14.73 (3.99)) or the Hayling test (overall scores 6.76 to 7.31, and no difference on the response-inhibition part); fluency error rates were at floor.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Prose recall, Fluency and Hayling test paragraphs (pp. 82–83); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: The abstract nevertheless lists category fluency among the frequent group's impairments (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: On the O-LIFE, unusual experiences differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 6.12, P < 0.001), higher in the frequent group than in all others (P < 0.05); cognitive disorganization (F(4, 145) = 4.81, P = 0.001) was higher in the frequent and infrequent groups than in the non-drug controls (P < 0.001); impulsive non-conformity (F(4, 145) = 3.96, P = 0.005) was higher in all four drug-using groups than in the non-drug controls (P < 0.01); introvertive anhedonia did not differ.
key_findings.note: Means appear only in Figure 3, whose axis starts at 1 (editors' reading: unusual experiences about 6.1 in the frequent group, about 4.3 in the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups, 3.3 in the polydrug and 2.4 in the non-drug controls).

key_findings.finding: Delusional ideation (PDI total) differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 8.40, P < 0.001): frequent 22.72 (14.10), infrequent 15.1 (10.33), ex-ketamine 15.79 (11.47), polydrug 13.03 (9.17), non-drug 9.43 (9.21); the paper reports the frequent group higher than all others (P < 0.05) and the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups higher than the non-drug controls (P < 0.01). Conviction (F(4, 145) = 2.73, P = 0.031) and preoccupation (F(4, 145) = 3.71, P = 0.007) were highest in the frequent group; distress did not differ.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 6 (one-way ANOVA, pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): F ≈ 5.9 rather than 8.40; P ≈ 0.27 (ex-ketamine) and 0.48 (infrequent) against the non-drug controls, and about 0.08 and 0.16 for the frequent group against the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups. The ex-ketamine and polydrug means were close (15.79 vs 13.03).

key_findings.finding: Dissociative experiences differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 6.60, P < 0.001): frequent 784 (451), infrequent 630 (408), ex-ketamine 401 (264), polydrug 488 (325), non-drug 321 (267); the frequent group was higher than all groups except the infrequent group (P < 0.01), and the infrequent group higher than the non-drug controls (P < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-report measures › Dissociative experiences scale (p. 83); Table 6 (p. 84)
key_findings.note: How the scale was scored is not described. Editors' calculation from Table 6: F ≈ 8.3 rather than 6.60.

key_findings.finding: Depressive symptoms (Beck Depression Inventory) differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 3.04, P = 0.019): frequent 11.48 (8.17), infrequent 9.03 (6.10), ex-ketamine 6.00 (5.11), polydrug 7.17 (5.38), non-drug 7.23 (7.00); the paper reports the frequent group higher than all others (P < 0.05). Trait anxiety did not differ (group means 31.17 to 36.03).
key_findings.locator: Results › Beck Depression Inventory (Table 6) and Speilberger Trait Anxiety scale (Table 6); Table 6
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 6 (pooled SD): frequent against infrequent P ≈ 0.14 without correction; against the polydrug and non-drug controls P ≈ 0.11 and 0.12 after Bonferroni correction; only the difference from the ex-ketamine group (P ≈ 0.01) is reproduced. The Discussion calls the frequent group's mean mild to moderate depression (p. 85) without giving cut-offs.

key_findings.finding: Within the frequent group, PDI total correlated with the current amount of ketamine per session (r = 0.433, P = 0.019); no other correlation between self-reported ketamine use and the key cognitive and symptom measures was significant, and amounts of cannabis, cocaine and amphetamine did not correlate with them. d′ correlated with spot-the-word (r = 0.474, P = 0.009), while years of education correlated with none of the cognitive measures.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Fisher z, n = 30): 95% CI 0.09 to 0.69 for r = 0.433. The number of correlations run is not stated.

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that the prose recall deficits found in their earlier studies, which tested people on the night of use and 3 days later, may simply reflect a lack of practice effects in the ketamine groups, and state that recreational use, on average 3 days per month here, was not associated with impaired cognitive function.

From the absence of deficits in the ex-ketamine group the authors infer that cognitive impairments may be reversible on stopping, noting that 8 of that group had used daily and that the group had used ketamine for longer than the others.
key_findings.note: The ex-ketamine group's frequency just before stopping (2.55 days per month) and its peak (11.21) were far below the frequent group's current 20.13 days (Table 2, p. 81).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that a study of this kind cannot rule out pre-existing group differences (p. 85), that the frequent group's greater family history of mental illness may have contributed to the findings, that only retesting the frequent group after a sufficient period of abstinence could show that deficits are reversible, and that the frequent group's cognitive impairments might reflect a withdrawal state (p. 86).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Psychological wellbeing, 1st paragraph (p. 85); Neurocognitive function, 5th paragraph, and Limitations (p. 86)

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states that the 19 people reporting daily use, some reporting up to 6 g per day, meet criteria for dependence, citing an earlier qualitative paper; the Method describes no measure of dependence.
key_findings.note: Claims about dependence in this sample cannot rest on this paper's own data.

key_findings.finding: The Introduction states, citing reference 9, that 3 days after taking part in a laboratory study, healthy volunteers who had received ketamine did not differ from those who had received placebo, and sets out three explanations for poorer memory in people who use ketamine when tested drug free: after-effects of taking the drug a few days earlier, differences that predate use, and long-lasting effects. It describes the less frequent group of Curran and Monaghan (2001) as using ketamine once a month.
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the laboratory study was not read for this card, and the team's papers cite two different laboratory reports for this finding (reporting issue 9). Curran and Monaghan (2001) give their less frequent group 0.45 days a month, about once every 2 months (that paper, pp. 753–754).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists category fluency among the frequent group's impairments (p. 77), but the Results report no group differences in category or letter fluency (p. 82), Table 5 shows the frequent group's category fluency (16.84) above the non-drug controls' (14.73) (p. 83), and the Discussion lists retrieval from semantic memory as unimpaired in this group (p. 85).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract cannot be cited for a category fluency deficit; the Results show none.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists a simple vigilance task among the cognitive tasks (p. 77), but no such task is described in the Method (p. 79) or reported in the Results (pp. 81–84).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either an outcome was measured and not reported, or the abstract is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the polydrug group as 22 men and 10 women, in a group the text and the other tables give as 30 (editors' calculation: the counts sum to 32).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the sex distribution of the polydrug controls cannot be stated with certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: Degrees of freedom do not match the sample: the hair comparison across five groups of 30 is printed as F(4, 149), and the comparison of years of use across three groups of 30 as F(2, 89) (editors' calculation: expected denominator df 145 and 87).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; suggests typing errors or different numbers analysed than stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of the frequent and infrequent groups gives Z = 1.81 with P = 0.003 for amount used and Z = 2.84 with P < 0.001 for days since last use (editors' calculation: two-tailed P for these Z values is about 0.07 and 0.005).
reporting_issues.consequence: The difference in amount per session between the frequent and infrequent groups may not be statistically significant as printed; at least one of each pair of numbers is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is internally inconsistent for the frequent group: a mean of 20.13 days per month with an SD of 2.36 is incompatible with daily use by 19 of 30 (if the 19 used ketamine on at least 28 days and the others on just over 4 days a week, the mean would be at least about 24 days; editors' calculation), and the same SD (2.36) is printed for the amount per session in the adjacent row. The frequent group's mean age at the start of regular use (25.90) exceeds its mean age (25.87, Table 1) although regular use is said to have lasted 5.03 years; in the ex-ketamine group, mean years of use (7.63) exceed the mean time since first use (27.3 minus 20.03, about 7.3 years) although the group had stopped a mean of 344 days earlier.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures for frequency and duration of use cannot all be right; claims should not rest on the frequent group's mean frequency or on durations of use from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: Several post hoc results cannot be reproduced from the printed means and SDs under the stated analysis (one-way ANOVA, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons; editors' calculation with the pooled within-group SD): d′ lower in the frequent group than in all others (only the ex-ketamine comparison reproduces); BDI higher in the frequent group than in all others (only the ex-ketamine comparison reproduces; against the infrequent group P ≈ 0.14 uncorrected); PDI total higher in the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups than in the non-drug controls at P < 0.01 (P ≈ 0.48 and 0.27); and the frequent group's SWM strategy against the polydrug controls (P ≈ 0.11). The omnibus F recomputed from Table 6 is about 5.9 for the PDI total (printed 8.40) and about 8.3 for the DES (printed 6.60).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claims that delusional ideation is elevated in infrequent and ex-ketamine use, and that the frequent group is worse than every other group on word recognition and depression, are not supported by the printed tables; either the tables or the tests are in error.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites reference 9 for an opportunistic study of 18 people who used ketamine (p. 85), but reference 9 is a laboratory study in healthy volunteers; the 18-person follow-up is reference 35 (Morgan et al., 2004) (p. 87).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation error; the 2004 follow-up is the study meant.

reporting_issues.issue: For the same first session, Morgan et al. (2010b) prints figures that differ from this paper's: the frequent group's days since last ketamine use, 2 (SD 2.60) against 1.6 (SD 1.27), range 1–7, here (2010b, Table 2, p. 125; here Table 2, p. 81); its Beck Depression Inventory score, 7.08 for the 25 retested against 11.48 for all 30 here, which can both hold only if the 5 not retested averaged about 33.5 (editors' calculation; 2010b, Table 4, p. 128; here Table 6, p. 84); and its amount per session (2.77 against 3.80 g) and the SD of its frequency of use (7.41 against 2.36 days a month), both for n = 30.
reporting_issues.consequence: Baseline values cannot be taken interchangeably from the two papers; claims that cite this paper's 1 to 7 days since last use or its depression score of 11.48 should note the other report (card sc_morgan_2010b, reporting issue 9).

reporting_issues.issue: The laboratory finding of no difference from placebo 3 days after a dose is cited to reference 9, the team's Psychopharmacology paper of 2004 (172, 298–308) (pp. 78, 87), whereas the team's 3-year follow-up attributes the same finding to its Neuropsychopharmacology paper of 2004 (29, 208–218), listed here as reference 3 (Morgan et al., 2004a, pp. 1451, 1457). Reference 9 is also cited on p. 85 for the 18-person follow-up (reporting issue 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which laboratory study shows no residual effect 3 days after a dose is unclear; claims should cite it only as the team's second-hand statement.

disagreements.first_pass: At least 24 hours from psychotropic drugs for drug-using participants, by self-report; urine results are not reported. The frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days (mean 1.6) after last ketamine use (Table 2, p. 81).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed: cigarettes were allowed during hourly breaks, the 24-hour abstinence from psychotropic drugs was self-reported, and the follow-up paper says it could not be verified biologically for this same session (Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 132).
disagreements.resolution: Verified at p. 79 (Procedure: 10-minute hourly breaks with a cigarette allowed) and in Morgan et al. (2010b), p. 132 (Discussion › Methodological considerations). Field extended.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed (cross-paper): for this same baseline session, Morgan et al. (2010b, Table 2, p. 125) gives the frequent group's days since last use as 2 (SD 2.60), range 1–14 (here 1.6 (1.27), range 1–7), and its BDI for the 25 retested as 7.08 (here 11.48 for all 30, which would need a mean of about 33.5 in the 5 not retested); a cross-reference would help, since claims cite the 1–7 days and the 11.48 from this paper.
disagreements.resolution: Verified here (Table 2, p. 81; Table 6, p. 84) and in Morgan et al. (2010b), Table 2 (p. 125, rendered at 220 dpi and rotated) and Table 4 (p. 128); arithmetic recomputed (33.48). Added as reporting issue 8, with the amount and frequency-SD differences that the 2010b card records; the bracketed (1–14) is not called a range, because that table's bracketed values are often not ranges (sc_morgan_2010b, reporting issue 5). Key finding 1 cross-refers.

disagreements.first_pass: A mean of 20.13 days per month with an SD of 2.36 cannot be reconciled with daily use by 19 of 30 (see reporting issues). Amount, frequency and days since last use differed between the frequent and infrequent groups (Z = 1.81, 3.87 and 2.84), with two Z–P pairs inconsistent (see reporting issues).

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed: the laboratory statement on p. 78 (Introduction, 3rd paragraph) matters for the night-of-use claim, which cites it second-hand from this paper; the paper also describes the less frequent group of Curran & Monaghan (2001) as using once a month.
disagreements.resolution: Verified at p. 78. The statement, which a claim anchor cites, had no key finding: added as key finding 17, with the description of the 2001 group checked against Curran & Monaghan (2001), pp. 753–754 (0.45 days a month).
